statement: Kernel-checked adaptive final theorem: if 0<theta<1 satisfies PI(theta), then every fixed 0<c<(1-theta)/3 gives the stated prime divisor for all sufficiently large k and 2k<n<=exp(c(log k)^2/loglog k). The older balanced 9/23 endpoint is an artifact. For the explicitly named location-blind, termwise-nonnegative full-tail certificate class, Lean proves the exact block invariant, PI cardinality tail, finite partition telescope, weighted good-block extraction, and a finite endpoint no-go uniform in family cardinality. Consequently even subdivisions whose finite block count grows arbitrarily with k cannot reach c>=(1-theta)/3 when the safe-tail and order-loss constants C,D are uniform and the summed nonnegative ledger is o(k^theta/log k). Lean also proves the leading LP equivalence LocationBlindTermwiseLeadingCertificate(theta,c) iff c<(1-theta)/3 for c>0. The source-geometric production of uniform C,D and the eventual limit instantiation remain explicit natural proof; Erdos 451 itself is not closed.

dependency_gaps: The abstract theta theorem assumes PI(theta); the theta=21/40 corollary imports the Baker--Harman--Pintz short-prime input exactly as the source paper does.

The complete adaptive four-range theorem is kernel-checked. For the enlarged no-go, the finite cardinality tail, partition telescope, weighted extraction, block algebra, and endpoint contradiction are kernel-checked uniformly over arbitrary finite index sets. The source-geometric derivation of fixed uniform comparison losses C,D and the eventual K/loglog(k)^2 separation are natural-proof instantiations rather than one formalized sequence theorem.

The no-go is confined to the named location-blind deterministic-tail class whose nonnegative Theorem 4.1 bounds are summed and required to be o(k^theta/log k). It does not cover sparse covers selected from actual prime locations, cross-block cancellation, stronger prime inputs, stronger exponential-sum estimates, or the true bad-set cardinality.
Novelty and publication priority remain unchecked.
